summary.title: An Investigation of the KF-type Lorentz-Symmetry Breaking Gauge Models in N = 1-Supersymmetric Scenario.
summary.authors: H. Belich, G. S. Dias, J.A. Helayel-Neto, F.J.L. Leal, W. Spalenza
summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates the incorporation of Kostelecky-Farnon (KF)-type Lorentz-symmetry violating (LV) electrodynamics into an N=1 supersymmetric framework. The authors propose two distinct mechanisms to accommodate the background tensor K_{\mu\nu\kappa\lambda}, which signals Lorentz violation, using either a chiral superfield or a vector superfield. The primary motivation is to explore the interplay between Lorentz symmetry breaking and supersymmetry (SUSY), hypothesizing that LV may be triggered by vacuum condensation of tensor fields at the Planck scale, a regime where SUSY imprints may persist. The study derives the component field actions for both scenarios, detailing the bosonic, fermionic, and coupled terms. In the chiral superfield case, the background is constrained such that the vector \xi^\mu is the gradient of a complex scalar S, leading to a specific form for the K-tensor dependent exclusively on S. In the vector superfield case, the background \xi^\mu is a component of a real vector superfield, allowing for a richer set of fermionic partners. The authors demonstrate that in both cases, the background breaks SUSY, as the SUSY transformations of the background fields do not vanish. The paper concludes by outlining future directions, including the analysis of photon-photino mass splitting and the potential for simultaneous spontaneous breaking of SUSY and Lorentz symmetry. The work provides a foundational supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model Extension (SME) gauge sector, offering new avenues for probing LV coefficients through supersymmetric partners.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates the incorporation of Kostelecky-Farnon (KF)-type Lorentz-symmetry violating (LV) electrodynamics into an N=1 supersymmetric framework. The authors propose two distinct mechanisms to accommodate the background tensor K_{\mu\nu\kappa\lambda}, which signals Lorentz violation, using either a chiral superfield or a vector superfield. The primary motivation is to explore the interplay between Lorentz symmetry breaking and supersymmetry (SUSY), hypothesizing that LV may be triggered by vacuum condensation of tensor fields at the Planck scale, a regime where SUSY imprints may persist. The study derives the component field actions for both scenarios, detailing the bosonic, fermionic, and coupled terms. In the chiral superfield case, the background is constrained such that the vector \xi^\mu is the gradient of a complex scalar S, leading to a specific form for the K-tensor dependent exclusively on S. In the vector superfield case, the background \xi^\mu is a component of a real vector superfield, allowing for a richer set of fermionic partners. The authors demonstrate that in both cases, the background breaks SUSY, as the SUSY transformations of the background fields do not vanish. The paper concludes by outlining future directions, including the analysis of photon-photino mass splitting and the potential for simultaneous spontaneous breaking of SUSY and Lorentz symmetry. The work provides a foundational supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model Extension (SME) gauge sector, offering new avenues for probing LV coefficients through supersymmetric partners.

Research Context
The Standard Model Extension (SME) is the natural framework to investigate properties of Lorentz-violation. The SME has been used to propose Lorentz-symmetry violation and CPT-probing experiments. The appearance of an anisotropic vacuum at Planck scale has drawn attention. Lorentz-symmetry and CPT invariance might be spontaneously broken in string theories. The authors adopt the viewpoint that breaking may be triggered by vacuum condensation. Supersymmetric partners are present even if SUSY had already been broken down. Lorentz-symmetry violation cannot be dissociated from SUSY in this fundamental level.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to accommodate KF-type Lorentz-symmetry violating Electrodynamics in an N=1-supersymmetric framework. The authors hypothesize that the background tensor K_{\mu\nu\kappa\lambda} can be expressed via chiral or vector superfields. It is predicted that the K-tensor will be determined by the components of the background superfield. The study aims to present actions with all fermionic partners of the background. The hypothesis is that SUSY is broken by the background fields in both scenarios. The authors propose to carry out the supersymmetric extension to the bosonic action. The expected outcome is a supersymmetric version of the K-type models.

Methodological Details
The study utilizes a covariant superspace-superfield formulation. Two possible venues are chosen: a chiral and a vector superfield. The chiral superfield \Omega is defined with a complex scalar S. The vector superfield \Xi is defined with a real vector \xi^\mu. The SUSY-covariant derivatives D_a and D_{\dot{a}} are defined explicitly. The Wess-Zumino gauge choice is taken for the gauge superpotential V. The background superfield \Omega is constrained to be chiral. The vector superfield \Xi is taken in its full \theta-expansion. The actions are decomposed into bosonic, fermionic, and coupled parts. The K-tensor symmetries are reduced using a specific ansatz.

Procedures And Architectures
The minimal extension for the chiral case is given by a specific superaction. The superaction involves the product of derivatives of \Omega and W. The component-wise counterpart for the chiral action is derived. The bosonic part of the chiral action includes terms with \partial S. The fermionic part of the chiral action involves \zeta and \lambda. The coupled part of the chiral action mixes gauge and background fields. The minimal extension for the vector case is given by another superaction. The vector superfield \Xi expansion includes C, \chi, M, \xi, \psi, B. The SUSY transformations for constant background components are simplified. The bosonic part of the vector action identifies the original K-tensor action.

Key Results
In the chiral case, the K-tensor depends exclusively on the scalar component S. A constant \partial^\mu S ensures the constancy of the K-tensor. The auxiliary field D is fixed to be non-trivial by the background. Charged scalar particles may acquire a magnetic dipole moment. In the vector case, the action reproduces the K-tensor defined by the ansatz. The vector case exhibits a richer background with more fermion condensates. SUSY is broken by the background in both chiral and vector cases. The supersymmetrization of the \xi^\mu \xi^\nu term automatically yields the \xi^\lambda \xi^\lambda term.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The chiral superfield imposes a special form for the K-tensor not yet discussed. The vector superfield allows for a richer set of partners. The breaking of Lorentz-symmetry signals the violation of SUSY. The model may descend from a more fundamental theory with spontaneous SUSY breaking. The study raises questions about the influence of LV on the spectrum. Restrictions are needed to avoid non-physical excitations like tachyons and ghosts. A future model could allow simultaneous spontaneous breaking of SUSY and Lorentz symmetry.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors do not have elements to decide if SUSY breaking occurred before LV. The analysis of photon-photino mass splitting is left for future work. The task of getting propagators demands special technicalities not fully worked out. The paper does not exploit the second way of working out supersymmetrization. The relation between SUSY and Lorentz-symmetry breakings remains a non-trivial question.

Claims
The KF-type Lorentz-symmetry breaking can be accommodated in N=1 SUSY using chiral or vector superfields. Two possible venues are presented to accommodate the KF-type Lorentz-symmetry violating Electrodynamics. A chiral and a vector superfield are chosen to describe the background. The authors do not have elements to decide whether SUSY breaking has occurred before LV. This provides a supersymmetric extension to the bosonic action.
The background fields break SUSY in both proposed scenarios. SUSY is readily seen to be broken by the background. The breaking of the latter signals the violation of the former. The authors do not state that they break Lorentz-symmetry and SUSY at the same time. Lorentz-symmetry breaking does not support exact SUSY.

Key Figures Tables
Equation (1) presents the bosonic action for the K-tensor model. Equation (7) presents the minimal extension for the chiral superfield. Equation (23) presents the minimal extension for the vector superfield.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the derivation of N=1 supersymmetric extensions for KF-type Lorentz-violating electrodynamics. 2. The strongest evidence is the explicit derivation of component field actions for both chiral and vector backgrounds. 3. The future path involves analyzing photon-photino mass splitting and simultaneous SUSY/Lorentz breaking.
